title: To stop escalation in the Black Sea, Turkey needs a new regional strategy
gist: Russia's escalating 2026 campaign against Greater Odesa's ports directly threatens Turkish shipping interests (roughly 40% of vessels calling there are Turkish-linked, and several Turkish-owned ships have been sunk or struck), yet Ankara's policy of treating Russian and Ukrainian maritime actions as equivalent is a false equivalence the author argues Turkey must abandon in favor of leading a harder regional deterrence framework with Romania and Bulgaria.

themes.theme: Scale of the Black Sea escalation

insights.claim: In the first half of 2026, Russia carried out more than 180 attacks on the ports of Greater Odesa (Odesa, Chornomorsk, and Pivdennyi), almost matching the total number of attacks for all of 2025, with July alone recording sixty-seven strikes on port facilities and an August 9 attack ranked among the largest on Odesa since 2022.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The attack rate roughly doubled year-over-year on an annualized basis, indicating a sharp, deliberate escalation in Russia's Black Sea campaign rather than a steady-state conflict pattern — relevant to shipping insurance and freight-risk pricing for the route.
insights.quote: In the first half of 2026, Russia carried out more than 180 attacks on the ports of Greater Odesa, almost matching the total for all of 2025.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Smoke rising on the horizon"

insights.claim: More than 90 percent of Ukraine's agricultural exports pass through its Black Sea ports; damage to port infrastructure is estimated at $1.5 billion since the war began, 90 percent of shipowners have suspended port calls, and alternative overland routes can absorb only around half of the cargo previously shipped by sea.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A near-total shipowner pullback (90%) combined with land routes covering only ~50% of prior volume implies Ukraine's effective agricultural export capacity may be cut by roughly half even accounting for rail/road substitution — a hard constraint for Ukrainian grain-export forecasts.
insights.quote: 90 percent of shipowners have suspended port calls

insights.claim: About 40 percent of vessels calling at Odesa-region ports are owned or operated by Turkish companies, according to the Black Sea Monitoring Group, putting substantial Turkish crews, fleets, and business interests directly in the line of fire.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Turkey has a direct commercial and casualty stake in Black Sea maritime security comparable to or exceeding some NATO allies with formal military involvement, reframing Turkish shipping and insurance sector exposure to the conflict.
insights.quote: about 40 percent of vessels calling at Odesa-region ports are owned or operated by Turkish companies
insights.locator: Turkey has skin in the game section

insights.claim: Since 2022, multiple Turkish-linked ships have been damaged in Russian attacks — including the Yasa Jupiter, Cenk T, Ant, Victress, and the LPG tanker Orinda — and in July 2026 the Turkish-owned cargo ship Golden Leo, carrying corn from Chornomorsk, was struck and sank off Odesa, killing ten.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A documented, growing casualty list of specific Turkish-flagged/owned vessels provides concrete precedent for rising war-risk insurance premiums and potential Turkish state pressure to escalate its own naval posture.

insights.claim: In August 2026, Turkish vessels Nadezhda and Yasar were attacked near Novorossiysk, injuring three crew members; Ankara called on both Russia and Ukraine to ensure navigation safety without establishing responsibility for the attack.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Illustrates Ankara's pattern of avoiding attribution even when its own vessels are hit, a policy stance the author argues obscures Russia's primary responsibility for the escalation.

insights.claim: Ankara's calls for 'both sides' to show restraint create a misleading picture of reciprocal escalation, when in fact Russia's sustained campaign against Ukrainian seaports, logistics infrastructure, and commercial ships receives comparatively less attention in Turkish media than Ukraine's own maritime operations.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: The author's core policy critique: Turkey should abandon symmetric-restraint diplomacy and instead differentiate Russian attacks on commercial shipping from Ukraine's targeted strikes on military-linked assets — a stance shift that would signal a harder Turkish posture toward Moscow.
insights.quote: Ankara should stop drawing a false equivalence between Ukraine’s strategy against military-linked targets and Russia’s attacks on legitimate commercial fleets.

insights.claim: According to Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, Ukrainian forces have struck 134 Russian vessels in the Sea of Azov and another eighty-four in the Black Sea, primarily targeting vessels tied to Russian military logistics, sanctions evasion, and wartime revenues.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Quantifies the scale of Ukraine's own maritime strike campaign (218 total vessels), useful context for assessing the relative intensity and targeting logic of each side's Black Sea operations.

insights.claim: According to the Financial Times, Ukraine halted attacks on tankers using the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal after an appeal from US Vice President JD Vance, while continuing to target Russian military and oil infrastructure elsewhere — showing Kyiv calibrates its strikes when allied economic interests are at stake.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Demonstrates Ukraine's strike campaign is politically responsive to US pressure on specific economic targets, a lever Washington has already used once and could use again to shape the scope of Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.

themes.theme: Spillover risk to NATO territory and energy infrastructure

insights.claim: Russian drones have repeatedly entered Moldovan, Romanian, and Turkish airspace, including one that crashed in Turkey's Izmit province near Istanbul, while in June 2026 a Ukrainian maritime drone lost control after Russian jamming and exploded in the Romanian port of Constanța, showing how Russian electronic interference can send Ukrainian systems off course onto NATO territory.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Russian jamming is creating unintended escalation risk by causing friendly (Ukrainian) systems to malfunction onto NATO soil — a distinct, harder-to-attribute spillover risk beyond direct Russian territorial violations.

insights.claim: Romania's Neptun Deep offshore gas project, located in Romania's exclusive economic zone, is approaching production in 2027 and is expected to produce around eight billion cubic meters of gas annually at peak output, strengthening Romanian and European energy security — a development Moscow is unlikely to welcome.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated (2027) new EU gas supply source that reduces European dependence on Russian gas — also a plausible future target for Russian hybrid or sabotage pressure given the stated Moscow displeasure.

insights.claim: Turkey's implementation of the Montreux Convention, which restricts warship movement through the Turkish Straits, has limited naval escalation, but the author argues regional ownership must also mean taking responsibility for deterring Russian aggression inside the Black Sea, not merely controlling who enters it.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Reframes the adequacy test for Turkey's Black Sea strategy: gatekeeping entry is necessary but insufficient; active deterrence of in-sea attacks is the higher bar Ankara is not yet meeting.
insights.quote: regional ownership cannot mean only controlling who enters the Black Sea. It must also mean taking responsibility for what happens inside it.
insights.locator: Regional ownership requires bold action section

insights.claim: At the 2026 NATO Summit in Ankara, Turkey, Romania, and Bulgaria amended a memorandum of understanding to expand the Mine Countermeasures Black Sea Task Group's mission to protect critical undersea infrastructure; the author recommends turning this into a broader trilateral naval patrol mission covering energy infrastructure, maritime trade, drone detection, and electronic-warfare defense.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
entities: Mine Countermeasures Black Sea Task Group
insights.so_what: A concrete, already-existing trilateral institutional vehicle (the Task Group) is available to be scaled up — watch for its expansion as a leading indicator of a more assertive Black Sea deterrence posture.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Trilaterally, Turkey, Romania, and Bulgaria"

insights.claim: The author recommends a potential transfer of US-made weapons from Turkish stocks to Ukraine as part of expanded US-Turkey-Ukraine cooperation on Black Sea maritime security.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: A specific, watchable policy option — Turkish stockpiles of US-made weapons transferred to Ukraine — that would represent a significant deepening of Turkish material support for Kyiv beyond its current mediator role.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Ankara should pursue these efforts"

insights.claim: The author argues there is no realistic return to the prewar Black Sea order, the 2023 grain deal, or a neutral maritime space insulated from the war, and that the only way to stop escalation is to increase the cost to Russia rather than pursue further neutrality-based diplomacy.
insights.speaker: Atlantic Council
insights.so_what: Explicitly rejects a return to a negotiated grain-corridor-style truce as the likely path forward, implying elevated and possibly prolonged shipping risk premiums for the Black Sea route rather than a near-term de-escalation deal.
insights.quote: The only way to stop escalation in the Black Sea is to increase the price for Russia.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning "Turkish mediation efforts remain important"
